items.title: U.S. Inflation Reaches 3.7% Ahead of Fed’s October Meeting | EconoTimes
items.excerpt: The Federal Reserve heads into its Oct. 27-28 meeting with U.S. consumer prices 3.7% higher than a year earlier, while a Reuters poll points to a possible December rate increase. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics said its Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers rose 3.7% in September from a year earlier, after a 3.4% annual increase in August. The Fed measures its 2% inflation objective using the personal consumption expenditures price index, rather than the CPI. The FOMC’s two-day policy session starts Tuesday, Oct. 27. The Fed’s target range is 3.75%-4.00%, following a 0.25 percentage-point increase in September. Reuters’ survey, conducted Oct. 16-20, found that 94 of 100 economists expected the Fed to leave the target range unchanged at this week’s meeting. All 100 respondents expected an increase at the Dec. 8-9 meeting. EconoTimes previously covered the survey’s unanimous outlook for a December rate increase.

items.title: Hot PPI and CPI data test Fed patience on rate hikes — NewsNovo
items.excerpt: U.S. inflationary pressures are broadening, testing the Federal Reserve's recent signals of patience on interest rates. Bureau of Labor Statistics data released this week shows price increases accelerating in both wholesale and consumer sectors, complicating the central bank's path ahead. The Producer Price Index rose 1.3% in September, the highest level since 2022 and far above the 0.6% analysts had expected. This followed a strong reading on consumer prices released Wednesday. Additionally, September retail sales increased by 0.8%, double the 0.4% forecast, while the August figure was revised upward. Initial claims for unemployment benefits stood at 199,000, remaining near historic lows. Nationwide financial market economist Oren Klachkin noted that the September PPI report reinforces the message from Wednesday's CPI data that inflation is moving in the wrong direction for the Fed. He added that businesses appear to be passing higher costs onto customers, as the proxy for margins rose significantly in September. Klachkin also pointed to AI-related categories as a source of upside pressure on prices. ... Fed Chair Jerome Powell faces a dilemma as he prepares for a policy meeting concluding on Oct. 28. In a speech at the International Monetary Fund's meetings in Thailand, Powell has a final opportunity to comment before the Fed enters its customary quiet period. Colleagues including New York Fed president John Williams and vice chair Philip Jefferson have signaled in recent weeks that they see little urgency to raise rates at a second consecutive meeting this month. ... If Powell affirms that stance despite the hot price data, it could raise doubts about his determination to bring inflation under control. Conversely, if he appears inclined to raise rates, he risks seeming overly reactive to a couple of economic releases, contrary to his stated goal of making the Fed less dependent on single data points. ... Market reactions have been mixed. Bond yields fell Thursday despite the hot PPI number, reversing a surge seen after Wednesday's CPI release. The policy-sensitive two-year Treasury yield briefly touched 4.95% after Wednesday's CPI data, implying significant Fed rate hikes ahead, before dropping to 4.72% Thursday morning. This move suggests a flight to quality among traders as optimism around the AI buildout fades and semiconductor stocks decline.

items.title: Trump's DOJ barrels into midterms with lawsuits, raids and arrests
items.excerpt: With just nine days until the midterms, the Trump administration is escalating its assault on two of the Department of Justice's most sacred guardrails: 1. Independence from the White House. 2. Restraint before elections. ... Why it matters: President Trump's DOJ has shattered the traditional calm of a pre-election period with a barrage of politically sensitive investigations, prosecutions and eleventh-hour efforts to influence the vote. ... Zoom in: The Justice Department's most aggressive election intervention yet came this week in Alaska, where a preemptive lawsuit seeks to delay certification of the state's U.S. Senate results — if the Democrat wins. - The DOJ argues that a second candidate, Dan J. Sullivan Jr., could confuse voters and siphon support from the Republican incumbent, Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. - The administration wants certification halted if Sen. Sullivan loses to Democrat Mary Peltola but could have won with votes cast for the other Sullivan, pending an investigation into voter intent. ... Between the lines: Alaska's Supreme Court already ruled that the second Sullivan belongs on the ballot, and the state's ranked-choice system allows voters to rank both candidates. - Legal experts question the DOJ's authority to block certification of a state-run election, or how officials could determine voters' intentions without compromising ballot secrecy. - Peltola's campaign and national Democrats have moved to intervene in the lawsuit, challenging the administration's preemptive attempt to halt certification. ... Zoom out: Alaska is just one front in an October offensive aimed at rooting out alleged election fraud, investigating prominent Democrats and relitigating Trump's oldest political grievances. ... - On Oct. 7, Trump established a White House committee to investigate alleged mortgage fraud by Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook, authorizing DOJ personnel to participate in proceedings that could lead to her removal. Cook denies wrongdoing. - On Oct. 12, federal agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar's (D-Minn.) home and seized her cellphone as part of an investigation into possible immigration fraud. The Wall Street Journal reports that the administration is building a case to try to strip the Somali-born lawmaker of her citizenship, and ultimately deport her. - On Oct. 15, DOJ sued California to block ballots from more than 20,000 suspected noncitizens. On Friday, prosecutors demanded that county officials segregate flagged ballots within 48 hours, warning of potential criminal liability. DOJ has also sought emergency appellate intervention. - On Oct. 22, prosecutors unveiled an eight-count indictment against Virginia state Sen. Louise Lucas — a key figure in Democrats' redistricting efforts in that state — alleging she helped operate an illegal marijuana enterprise. Lucas denies wrongdoing. - On Oct. 23, two former senior FBI officials were charged with lying to Congress about their roles in the Hunter Biden investigation. FBI Director Kash Patel cast the arrests as part of a crackdown on alleged political "weaponization" against Trump.

items.title: Nerd News: Cliff Booth, Clayface & MCR (10/25/2026)
items.excerpt: Saturday delivered one of those entertainment cycles where the strangest story somehow involved the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders, My Chemical Romance and a courtroom. Before we got there, Quentin Tarantino surprised an AFI Fest crowd with the first 17 minutes of The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, providing the first extended look at David Fincher’s continuation of Once Upon a Time in Hollywood. DC Studios also appears to have another theatrical win with Clayface, Paramount+ moved another step closer to being folded into HBO Max’s creative structure, and Charli xcx added Martin Scorsese to an increasingly ridiculous list of filmmakers she has worked with. ... Brad Pitt returns as Cliff Booth in a story set in 1977, eight years after the events of Once Upon a Time in Hollywood. Tarantino wrote the screenplay while David Fincher directs, creating one of the stranger filmmaker combinations in recent memory. The new movie positions Cliff as a Hollywood fixer who spends part of his time working at the New Beverly Cinema while dealing with situations requiring the kind of morally flexible problem-solving that made him so memorable the first time around. ... DC Studios’ Clayface is headed toward an estimated $24 million domestic opening after earning approximately $10.4 million on Friday.

items.title: Charli xcx Joins Martin Scorsese's 'What Happens at Night'
items.excerpt: Sources tell Variety that the pop star has a cameo in the Oscar-winning director’s upcoming movie “What Happens at Night” alongside Leonardo DiCaprio and Jennifer Lawrence. Described as a Gothic psychological drama, the Apple and StudioCanal production follows an American married couple who travel to a small European town to adopt a baby — but as they struggle to claim their child, the less they seem to know about themselves. Charli’s part in the film is being kept under wraps. She joins a cast that also includes Mads Mikkelsen, Patricia Clarkson and Jared Harris.

items.title: HYBE Cine Fest 2026 Cinema Event Going Global With 2 Live BTS Broadcasts
items.excerpt: The HYBE Cine Fest is going international this year with a weeklong global event hitting theaters in more than 60 territories from Oct. 24-31. After launching in Latin America in 2024 and expanding to Asia in 2025, this year’s collaboration between Trafalgar Releasing and HYBE will feature six different events, including the first-ever airings of two BTS live broadcasts from South America. The BTS WORLD TOUR ‘ARIRANG’ in Buenos Aires: Live Viewing in cinemas will mark the K-pop supergroup’s first-ever performance in Argentina, with screenings slated for Oct. 24 in the Americas and Oct. 25 in the rest of the world. A second BTS show, ARIRANG in SÃO PAULO: Live Viewing, will mark the grand finale of the boy band’s Latin American tour, with screenings slated for Oct. 30 in the Americas and Oct. 31 in the rest of the world.
